title: The African church
hookLine: from an Ethiopian official on a desert road to packed churches across the continent, the map of Christianity has shifted south

lines: A CHARIOT ON A DESERT ROAD.
cards: A chariot is rolling along the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem toward Gaza. In it sits a royal treasurer from the court of the queen of the Ethiopians, heading home after worshiping in Jerusalem.

A scroll of Isaiah is open on his knees, and he's reading aloud. A man named Philip runs up alongside and calls out, in the King James Bible: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The official invites him up.
Further on, they pass some water, and the official says: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" The African church starts earlier than some people expect.

teach.h: AFRICAN FROM THE BOOK OF ACTS.
teach.b: That Ethiopian official goes home baptized, in the eighth chapter of Acts, and the Bible never mentions him again. But Africa doesn't leave the story.
Egypt's Coptic Christians trace their church, by tradition, to Mark, the Gospel writer.

Some early Christian writers came from North Africa, Augustine among them. Ethiopia has its own ancient church, with scriptures in the old language Ge'ez and churches carved straight down into the rock.
So when people call Christianity a Western religion that arrived in Africa with Europeans, the Bible itself and these old churches answer back. Then came a harder chapter.
European missionaries arrived alongside colonial rule, and the two got tangled; schools, hospitals and translated Bibles came with land taken and cultures dismissed.

Historians of African Christianity also stress that much of the spreading was done by Africans themselves, catechists, evangelists, prophets and ordinary converts, often far beyond any missionary's reach.
Some started churches of their own, African independent churches, praying in their own languages and music.
Today the continent is full of church life: Anglicans in Nigeria and Uganda, Catholics in Congo, Orthodox in Ethiopia, Pentecostals in Ghana and Kenya, and many more.

Some who study world Christianity say its center of gravity has moved south, away from Europe and North America. And traffic now runs both ways: some African churches plant congregations in London, Houston and Berlin.
Some readers see the treasurer on the desert road as an early sign of where the story was heading.

how: African churches range from the ancient Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo and Coptic Orthodox churches to Catholic, Anglican, Protestant, Pentecostal and African independent churches. Worship is commonly in local languages, with music, singing and dancing.

games.why: he invites Philip up, they talk about Isaiah, and when they come to some water he asks to be baptized.

practice: Travel the continent in thought: a Coptic church in Cairo, a stone church in the Ethiopian highlands, a cathedral in Kampala, a big Pentecostal gathering in Lagos, then any African congregation meeting in your own city.
Stop at one and listen: a choir, a drum, a language you may not know. If you pray, pray for that church and its people; if you don't, send them good will in the quiet.
